description: We are a multidisciplinary team of five from the University of Málaga: robotics, mechanics, programming, economics and design. We are building Stars Beside You, a tool that uses NASA data to find places on Earth that resemble lunar sites. We are friendly, curious and love learning from each other. We would love to meet people with skills in GIS, remote sensing, data science, planetary science or web and UX design. Whatever your level, join us!
summary:
Welcome to Stars Beside You! For this NASA challenge, the project is not just a tool: it is a finder for places on Earth that resemble the Moon. Before a rover, a solar panel or a habitat system touches the lunar surface, it has to prove that it works. But where is it tested? Until now, the site has usually been chosen by experience and instinct.

Stars Beside You changes that. Using real NASA data, it compares the Moon with thousands of points across the planet and looks for the ones that resemble it most. Users choose the type of mission, adjust what matters most to them with simple sliders, and the map instantly shows them where to test it.

It is not just a map: it is a way to put NASA’s open data in the hands of any team, big or small, so they can decide where to test with clear criteria, transparency and less uncertainty. Because to reach the Moon, you first have to find its reflection on Earth.
details:
Stars Beside You is a web app that answers one question: where on Earth can I test my lunar mission?

For each of three Moon missions (Rover, Solar panels and Lunar base), it lists places on Earth where the mission can be tested because they resemble a place on the Moon, and it names that lunar place, which we call the lunar twin. Every value shown carries its source and its data level: measured, derived or modelled.

It is meant for mission and test planners, students and the public.

How it works

  1. Choose a mission. The user picks Rover, Solar panels or Lunar base, by clicking or by pressing 1, 2 or 3. It works on desktop and phone.
  2. Two 3D globes. The Earth and the Moon appear as interactive globes covered with candidate points. The Earth uses NASA satellite imagery and the Moon uses the LRO camera mosaic.
  3. Top 5 sites. A ranking lists the five best places on Earth for the chosen mission, each with its lunar twin.
  4. Select a point. Clicking a site shows the lunar place it matches, with the reasons and the source of every number.

Behind the scenes

Real data on both bodies. Everything is built on real 1-degree tables.

  • Moon: NASA LRO LOLA (terrain), Diviner (temperature and rock abundance) and solar illumination.
  • Earth: NOAA ETOPO (terrain), ESA land cover, NASA MODIS temperature, WorldClim climate, permafrost maps and ISCCP cloud data.

Pairing engine. Each Earth point must first pass the mission’s hard filters. It then receives a final score: 50% similarity to its lunar twin and 50% suitability for the mission. The twin is searched in a different lunar zone for each mission:

Mission

Earth side

Lunar twin

Matched on

Rover

Flat, smooth, bare ground

South-polar rover zone (latitude -75° or lower)

Slope and roughness

Solar panels

Sunny, flat ground with clear skies

Low equatorial plains (the maria)

Sunlight above the atmosphere, slope, roughness

Lunar base

Cold places with a strong daily thermal swing (at least 15 K)

One of NASA’s nine candidate landing regions near the south pole

Thermal position, slope, roughness

Differences smaller than the elevation models’ own measurement error count as equal, so the tool never claims more precision than the data has. The five sites shown are spread across the world, at least 2 degrees apart for Solar panels and Lunar base.

Benefits

  • Objective site selection instead of relying only on experience.
  • Fewer exploratory campaigns: thousands of candidates are narrowed to a few justified ones.
  • Transparency: every number shows its source and data level, and every threshold and assumption is documented.
  • Accessibility: open data, no account or API key needed, and a static site anyone can open from a link.
  • Economic case: our economic analysis shows why testing at Earth analogs pays off, since testing in space costs 3 to 40 times more. It includes a 4-page report, a 17-sheet workbook and every source URL.

Intended impact

To give mission planners, universities, startups and space agencies a first, evidence-based filter for choosing where to test lunar equipment, and to make NASA’s open data understandable to students and the public. The same approach could extend to Mars and other bodies.

Tools and technologies

  • Web app: TypeScript, Vite and CesiumJS (3D globes), deployed on Vercel as a static site.
  • Analog engine and data pipeline: Python (numpy, pandas, scipy, pydantic, rasterio, pyproj, netCDF4), with a pytest test suite.
  • Data: NASA PDS (LRO LOLA and Diviner), NOAA ETOPO, ESA CCI land cover, NASA MODIS, WorldClim, PANGAEA permafrost maps and NOAA ISCCP.
  • Imagery: NASA GIBS, Sentinel-2 cloudless (EOX) and NASA Moon Trek.
  • Mission videos: 3D simulations rendered with three.js.
  • Audio guide: 19 short tracks recorded with a text-to-speech service.

What makes it creative

  • Every Earth site comes with a named lunar twin. The test is linked to a specific place on the Moon, not to a generic idea of “moon-like terrain”.
  • Each mission defines its own twin. A rover looks for polar terrain, solar panels for equatorial plains, and a lunar base for NASA’s candidate landing regions.
  • Two planets in one framework, side by side in 3D.
  • Nothing is a black box. Each number states its source and whether it is measured, derived or modelled.
  • It is experienced, not just read: keyboard shortcuts, mission videos, an audio guide and a phone-friendly interface.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific honesty. Data levels, tolerances based on measurement error, and a statistical audit and validation document in the repository.
  • Reproducibility. The engine, real-data builders and tests are all in the repository and documented.
  • Licensing. Every source is credited with its licence in the app.
  • Accessibility. No account, no API key, works on desktop and phone.
  • Economics. We assessed the value of testing on Earth instead of in space.

Limitations

  • The data is on a 1-degree grid, so it supports choosing regions, not exact test sites.
  • Some variables are derived or modelled, not measured, and are labelled accordingly.
  • The tool compares terrain, sunlight and temperature, and does not model gravity, radiation or vacuum.
  • The mission videos are simulations, not real footage, and each one says so.
  • WorldClim data is free for non-commercial use only, so commercial reuse would need permission.
